--- title: "Why optimal-excitation system ID" description: "A balanced, evidence-based case for optimal-excitation frequency-domain identification (Pintelon–Schoukens) against broadband random noise and swept sine — with real head-to-head campaigns from the system_ident package, and an honest account of when each alternative is the right choice." freeze: true --- This page makes the case for the measurement method `system_ident` implements — an **optimal-excitation, periodic-multisine, frequency-domain** identification in the [Pintelon–Schoukens](overview.qmd) ("P&S") tradition — and weighs it fairly against the two excitations most subsystems reach for first: **broadband random noise** and the **swept sine**. It is written for engineers in *any* LIGO subsystem — suspensions, seismic/ISI, DARM/calibration, ALS, OMC — because the argument is about the measurement, not the plant. The thesis is not "multisine always wins." It is: **when measurement time is expensive, drive is bounded, the plant is high-Q, and the loop is closed, optimal-excitation ID buys you more parameter precision per second and per count of drive than the alternatives — and we can show it, not just assert it.** Where a swept sine or random noise is the right tool, this page says so. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Everything below is a real package run Every number and figure comes from the glue module `docs/method_demo.py`, which runs the campaigns through the library internals (`SysIDLoop._estimate_tf_periodic`, `optimal_excitation`, `fisher.parameter_covariance`, `run_siso_passes`). The page is rendered with `freeze: true`. No number on this page is hand-entered; if a result is mixed, the text says so. ::: ::: {#fce9a75d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue (runs the real campaigns)"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "method_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "method_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np from IPython.display import display import method_demo as md ``` ::: ## 1 · The measurement problem, and the figures of merit Every subsystem identification looks the same once you squint: a plant with **sharp, high-Q resonances** packed into a **narrow band**, observed through a **noisy readout**, driven by an actuator with a **hard amplitude limit**, often **inside a closed loop** — and you get only so much **observing time** to measure it before the instrument must go back to work. ::: {#2651162a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="A representative suspension plant over its readout floor"} md.problem_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: So a method is good or bad only relative to what you actually pay and get. We score every excitation on the same five figures of merit: - **Parameter / FRF uncertainty per unit time** — the Cramér–Rao σ (or σ/θ) reached for a given total measurement time. *Less time for the same σ is the prize.* - **Uncertainty per unit drive** — the same σ for a given **peak** and **RMS** drive. Drive is capped by actuator saturation, so this is a hard currency too. - **Leakage bias** — does the estimator read a sharp resonance at its true height, or smear it? A bias no amount of averaging removes. - **Per-bin noise model** — does the method *measure* its own error bar on each frequency, or must you assume one? - **Safety** — the **peak drive** the method puts on the actuator, and whether it is safe to run **closed-loop**. The rest of this page is those five columns, filled with real numbers. ## 2 · The three excitations, fairly All three put energy into the plant and watch it respond. They differ in *how the energy is distributed in frequency and time* — and that difference is the whole story. ::: {#b4349fd5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="The same in-band power as swept sine, random noise, and a multisine"} md.excitations_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - **Swept sine** drives **one frequency at a time**, dwelling long enough to beat down noise at that line. It is leakage-free per line, trivially interpretable, and spends *all* its power where it is pointed — but it visits the band **serially**. - **Broadband random noise** drives **every frequency at once** with random phase. It is the fastest way to a qualitative whole-band picture and an honest coherence — but its **random phase gives a large crest factor** (so it saturates sooner for the same RMS), it is **not periodic** (so its DFT leaks), and a single record gives no internal error bar. - **Periodic multisine** also drives every frequency at once, but with **deterministic (Schroeder) phases** that minimise the crest factor and, crucially, with a period **exactly equal to the analysis window**, tiled and repeated. That periodicity is what makes the measurement leakage-free and self-error-barred — and it is the substrate the optimal design shapes. The crest factors printed above are real: the Schroeder multisine carries the same in-band power as the random drive at a markedly lower peak — the first of its advantages under a hard actuator limit. ## 3 · Broadband random noise leaks, and is variance-inefficient The case against random noise is not aesthetic. On a **high-Q resonance** — exactly where the information lives — a windowed transform of a one-off random record **biases the peak low**, because the sharp mode leaks its power into neighbouring bins. The leakage-free multisine, given **the same plant, the same power, and the same wall-clock**, does not. ::: {#1be56d6b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Same high-Q mode, same power, same time: leakage-free vs windowed random"} c_leak = md.leakage_campaign(seed=0) md.leakage_bode_fig(c_leak) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The multisine markers sit on the true peak with tight error bars; the windowed-Welch points read the resonance visibly low. Repeating both over several noise realisations separates the two failure modes — **bias** (leakage) and **scatter** (variance): ::: {#7866dcef .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Peak-bin bias and scatter over several seeds"} v_leak = md.leakage_variance(n_seeds=8) display(md.leakage_table(v_leak)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **High-Q peak recovery (Q=60, linewidth ≈2.1 bins): the random estimator is biased AND noisier — combined it is 31× worse at the peak** | peak-bin figure of merit | leakage-free multisine | windowed random (Welch) | truth | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | peak-bin estimate (mean) | 453.5 | 381.1 | 455.9 | | bias vs truth | -0.5% | -16.4% | 0 | | scatter (std, 8 seeds) | 0.00 | 20.30 | — | | peak RMSE (bias+scatter) | 2.47 | 77.54 | — | ::: ::: The random estimator is biased **and** noisier; combined as RMSE at the peak it is many times worse than the leakage-free multisine carrying identical power for identical time. This is the single most important reason the package never identifies with random noise: the bias is systematic, it lands exactly on the high-Q features you care most about, and **averaging longer does not remove it.** ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## When random noise *is* the right tool For a **qualitative** whole-band look, a quick **coherence** check, or any broadband floor/ disturbance characterisation where a percent-level peak bias is irrelevant, colored random noise is fast, simple, and entirely appropriate — and `excitation.timeseries_from_asd` exists for exactly that. The argument here is against using it as the *quantitative FRF estimator* on a sharp resonance. ::: ## 4 · The swept sine is slow The swept sine has no leakage problem and no crest-factor problem — it spends full power on one clean line at a time. Its cost is **time**: it tours the band **serially**. The multisine measures **every bin in one window**; in that *same* wall-clock the sweep reaches only a handful of frequencies (each, fairly, very tight because it spends full power there). ::: {#44f0f5c8 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="σ(FRF)/|FRF| — whole-band multisine vs equal-wall-clock swept sine"} c_sweep = md.sweep_campaign(seed=0) md.sweep_fig(c_sweep) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The sweep points sit *on or below* the multisine envelope — full power per line buys low σ at each visited frequency — but there are only a few of them. **Covering the whole band to the same per-bin σ costs the sweep the factor annotated on the plot** (here roughly two orders of magnitude longer than the one multisine window). On a real instrument that is the difference between a measurement that fits inside a maintenance window and one that does not. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## When the swept sine *is* the right tool For a **single line** — one calibration tone, one resonance you want pinned to high SNR, a quick spot check — the swept sine is the obvious choice: nothing beats putting all your power on the one frequency you care about. It is also the most transparent thing to interpret. The multisine wins when you need **the whole band**. ::: ## 5 · Optimal excitation wins on time *and* on drive (the headline) So far the multisine has matched the alternatives where they are weak. The headline result is where it is *strong*: spend the drive budget not flat across the band, but **concentrated where the Fisher information is**. `design.pintelon.optimal_excitation` solves for that allocation by the dispersion-function fixed point (see [Fisher & excitation](fisher.qmd)). ::: {#086b3ce7 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="The optimal drive concentrates power at the modes; CRB variance-reduction F"} head = md.headline_campaign() md.headline_design_fig(head) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The gold drive piles power onto the two resonances instead of spreading it flat. The exact **Cramér–Rao variance-reduction factor** `F` — worst-parameter, at equal power and time, from `fisher.parameter_covariance` — is annotated on the design panel. That factor is the budget the optimal design has to spend, and it can be cashed out **two** ways: ::: {#7f77760f .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Three real campaigns: flat, optimal (same power), optimal (matched σ)"} md.headline_convergence_fig(head) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#48347005 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Head-to-head: σ reached, and the drive it took"} display(md.headline_table(head)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Same plant, same 4 passes. At equal power the optimal drive reaches 5.0× lower σ; dialled to P/F it MATCHES flat's σ at 1.9× less peak and 3.8× less RMS drive (F=14 from the CRB)** | excitation | drive power | peak drive | RMS drive | final σ/θ | passes to σ/θ≤0.05 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | flat multisine | P | 1.85 | 1.00 | 0.074 | — | | optimal multisine | P | 3.56 | 1.00 | 0.015 | 2 | | optimal multisine | P/14 | 0.95 | 0.27 | 0.055 | — | ::: ::: Read the table honestly, both rows of the optimal arm: - **At equal drive power**, the optimal multisine reaches a parameter uncertainty several times lower than the flat drive in the same number of passes — the flat drive never even crosses the σ/θ target inside the budget, while the optimal drive crosses it in a couple of passes. *That is the time win.* (Its **peak** is higher than flat's, because concentrating power raises the crest factor — stated plainly, not hidden.) - **Dialled down to power P/F**, the optimal multisine instead *matches* the flat drive's σ — but now at a fraction of the **peak** and **RMS** drive. *That is the drive win:* the same answer for materially less force on the actuator. You do not get both at once for free — `F` is one budget — but you get to **choose** which scarce resource (time or drive) to spend it on. Flat excitation gives you neither choice. ## 6 · A closed loop is not an obstacle Most LIGO plants are measured **inside a control loop** — the very damping or servo that keeps the instrument usable suppresses the response you want to see. The naive FRF taken against the *injected reference* then returns the **suppressed closed-loop response**, not the plant. The P&S **reference-based** estimate — the ratio of period-averaged spectra against the **drive monitor** (the true plant input) — cancels the controller and returns the **open-loop plant**, with no controller model. ::: {#a174f8d0 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="A high-Q mode under a velocity damper: recover the open-loop plant through the live loop"} cl = md.closed_loop_campaign(seed=0) md.closed_loop_fig(cl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The loop suppresses the resonance by the factor in the title, and the naive estimate dutifully returns that suppressed curve. The reference-based estimate, against the same data, lands back on the **open-loop** plant to a fraction of a percent — the controller is *cancelled, not fit*. This is why "the plant is in a loop" is not a reason to reach for special-case tooling: the same multisine pipeline handles it. (The DARM page, [example 08](../examples/08-darm-calibration.qmd), is the same idea on the gravitational-wave readout; the suspension closed loop here is the general statement.) ## 7 · The consolidated head-to-head One table, four excitations, the five figures of merit — populated from the real campaigns above on the representative suspension plants of this page. ::: {#77173ef5 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Everything, side by side (real numbers from the campaigns)"} display(md.headtohead_table(head, v_leak, c_sweep, cl)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Head-to-head on the representative suspension plants of this page. Peak/RMS for the optimal arm are at the budget that MATCHES flat's σ (F=14); the closed-loop reference FRF recovered the open-loop plant to 1.4% through a 48× suppressing loop.** | excitation | time to target σ | peak drive | RMS drive | leakage bias (high-Q peak) | per-bin noise model? | closed-loop safe? | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | swept sine | ~122× a multisine window | high (1 line) | 1.00 | none (1 line) | per-line coherence | yes, but slow | | broadband random | never (biased) | ≈3.7 (random φ) | 1.00 | -16% (leaks) | no (assumed) | no (S_yx/S_xx biased) | | flat multisine | > budget passes | 1.85 | 1.00 | -1% (leakage-free) | yes (period scatter) | yes (reference-based) | | optimal multisine | 2 passes | 0.95 | 0.27 | -1% (leakage-free) | yes (period scatter) | yes (reference-based) | ::: ::: The pattern: the swept sine is safe and exact but slow; broadband random is fast but biased on the high-Q peaks and unsafe to use as the quantitative estimator in a loop; the flat multisine fixes leakage and the loop but spends its budget indiscriminately; the **optimal multisine** keeps every multisine advantage and additionally converts the Fisher structure of the plant into **less time or less drive, your choice.** ## 8 · How any subsystem uses the package The pipeline is plant-agnostic. To identify a new subsystem you supply two things — a **channel backend** (how to inject and read) and a **prior model** — and run the loop: ```python from system_ident.backends.base import ChannelBackend # implement inject()/read()/ramp_down() from system_ident.backends.twin import TwinBackend # or the provided twin/CDS/DARM backends from system_ident.model import TFModel from system_ident.loop import SysIDLoop from system_ident.design.pintelon import PintelonSchoukensDesigner from system_ident.estimators.gml import GMLEstimator from system_ident.safety import Watchdog, SafetyLimits # 1. a prior — even a rough one; the first pass is prior-robust over f0·(1±u) prior = {"POS": TFModel.from_resonances([(1.0, 50.0)], gain=300.0)} # 2. a backend that speaks your channels (twin shown; swap in your CDS/hardware backend) backend = TwinBackend(plant, {"EXC": "POS"}, {"RSP": "POS"}, drive_channels={"DRV": "POS"}) # DRV = the loop's drive monitor # 3. the loop wires designer + estimator + watchdog and runs: # measure noise → design optimal multisine → inject (Schroeder, Tukey-ramped) # → leakage-free reference FRF → ML fit → CRB → redesign → repeat loop = SysIDLoop(backend, GMLEstimator(), PintelonSchoukensDesigner(), Watchdog(SafetyLimits.from_config(config))) result = loop.run(config, prior, seed=0) # result.models["POS"] is the fit ``` Everything on this page is that loop with a different `config` and `prior`. The worked [examples 01–08](../examples/index.qmd) walk the same path from a single resonance through a coupled 2×2 suspension, the compiled CDS twin, and the DARM readout — each running the *identical* diagnostic set (excitation design → time series → magnitude/phase/coherence Bode → residuals → Cramér–Rao recovery → drive safety → convergence). ## 9 · Honest caveats — and when each alternative is right No method is free. The optimal multisine carries real assumptions and failure modes, and the alternatives are genuinely better in specific regimes. **What the optimal multisine needs.** - **Synchronous, integer-period capture.** The leakage-free guarantee holds only if the drive is periodic over the analysis window and the acquisition is sample-synchronous. Lose period alignment (clock drift, dropped samples, a non-integer window) and the leakage advantage decays toward the windowed-random case. On CDS this is a wiring requirement, not a given. - **A prior.** The optimal design is only as good as the model it is computed from. The package mitigates this with a **prior-robust first pass** (power spread over `f0·(1±u)`), but a wildly wrong prior, an over-specified model order, or a missing mode can misallocate the budget. The honest mode of operation is *iterative*: a broad pass, then concentrate. - **A stationary, linear plant over the window.** The whole-band-in-one-window advantage assumes the plant does not drift mid-measurement and responds linearly to the drive. Strong nonlinearity or fast non-stationarity breaks the model the CRB is computed against. - **In a comb-sensitive band, a comb is a cost.** A multisine puts many lines in band at once. Where those lines contaminate a science band (e.g. DARM during observation), that footprint is a real operational price the swept sine's single line largely avoids — run in non-observing time, or use known phases so the lines subtract. **When to pick the alternative instead.** - **Swept sine** — a single line to high SNR, a quick spot check, or any time transparency and putting all power on one frequency matter more than band coverage. - **Broadband random** — a fast qualitative whole-band picture, coherence diagnostics, or disturbance/floor characterisation where a percent-level peak bias is irrelevant. - **Flat multisine** — when you have *no* usable prior at all and want leakage-free, self-error- barred whole-band coverage before you know where to concentrate. (It is the package's own first pass.) The optimal multisine is the right default when **all** of: time is scarce, drive is bounded, the plant is high-Q, the loop is closed, and you have at least a rough prior — which is to say, most of the time, on most LIGO subsystems. But the package implements **one** pipeline, and the honest position is to know which knob (and which excitation) the situation calls for. ## References Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*, 2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 — periodic / leakage-free measurement; multisine design and Schroeder phases (§4); dispersion-function optimal input design (§5.4.2); the reference-based (closed-loop) FRF; and the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimator with its Cramér–Rao efficiency. [LIGO-G2101503](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G2101503) — Fisher-information expressions for suspension parameters (the form carried by `fisher.fisher_matrix`). [LIGO-G1400084](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G1400084) (Larry Price) — original motivation and prior work. See also `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md` for the DARM-specific head-to-head and its literature trail.
